headline: A value is judged by what it is, an actor by which field named it, and a limit only binds when it is a number
summary: Three questions were being answered by the wrong test. Whether a value is bytes was answered by `instanceof`, which compares against one realm's constructor. Whether a value can be serialized was answered by a list of type names, which missed five types that serialize to an empty object. Whether a limit is exceeded was answered against a value nothing had checked was a number, and every comparison with a non-number is false. A fourth ran alongside them: which principal an action belongs to was answered by reading whichever identity field a caller happened to use, so principals that the framework's own resolver separates were folded together. Each had a case where the wrong answer was to skip work rather than refuse it, and those are the entries under Security.

items.title: A CSV export under a redacting posture redacts
items.body: `b.guardCsv.serialize` read `piiPolicy: "redact"` as "redact if the caller also passed `opts.redact`", and the HIPAA, PCI-DSS and GDPR postures all set that policy. An operator who selected a posture and wrote no redactor of their own got the rows back whole: measured under the HIPAA posture, a Social Security number and a Luhn-valid card number both reached the output. The policy now scrubs every emitted string cell with `b.redact.redactText`, which removes SSNs, card numbers, JWTs, PEM blocks, AWS keys and URL passwords and leaves the surrounding text. `opts.redact` still replaces it, and a value carrying no `string(value)` method is refused rather than ignored.

items.title: An idempotency key cannot answer two principals from one cache entry
items.body: The default scope read `actor.userId` and folded every other actor onto the literal `"anon"`. `extractActorContext` fills `userId` from `req.user.id`, `req.user.userId` or `req.apiKey.ownerId` only, so a bearer token carrying `sub`, the ordinary OIDC shape, left every principal on that literal. Two authenticated users sending the same idempotency key were answered from one cache entry: measured, the second received the first's status, headers and body verbatim. An actor the request carries is now scoped by `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey`, which tags the key with the field it came from so `id:"x"` and `sub:"x"` cannot collide, and refuses an actor it cannot name rather than folding it onto a shared literal. A request carrying no actor keeps the shared anonymous scope, because the middleware cannot tell two anonymous callers apart by construction.

items.title: A step-up grant binds to the principal that holds it, not to one field's text
items.body: `b.middleware.requireStepUp` matches a grant's subject against `req.user.id`, then `userId`, then `claims.sub`, then `sub`. A grant carried only the text, so every principal named by any of those four fields with the same text held the same grant: measured, one grant minted for `"collide"` elevated all four of `{ id }`, `{ userId }`, `{ claims.sub }` and `{ sub }`. `b.auth.stepUp.grant.create({ actor: req.user })` mints a grant bound to the field that names the principal as well as to the value, and the middleware passes the request's actor so the check runs against that binding. Such a grant is refused for a principal named by a different field, and refused outright when the caller checks it without naming an actor, rather than falling back to the text. `create` refuses an actor and a subject together, and refuses an actor that names no principal. `{ subject: "..." }` is unchanged and keeps matching the resolver's chain.

items.title: A break-glass grant, an unseal-rate bucket and a static quota window each name one principal
items.body: Four per-actor buckets derived identity by reading fields inline, and each folded principals that `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` separates. `b.breakGlass` records a grant's holder as `user:<userId>` or `apikey:<keyId>`; a user whose `userId` spelled an API key's id produced the same holder text, so `listActive` returned each of them the other's live grant ids, and `unsealRow` redeems a grant from its id alone. That same text keyed the factor lockout and the TOTP replay-step reservation. `revokeAll` now takes either prefix to target one holder and a bare id to reach both, and refuses when the grants table carries no derived owner hash, where it previously dropped the actor criterion and revoked by table alone, or revoked every active grant when no table was named.

items.title: A sealed-column read names the principal its unseal-failure cap counts for
items.body: `b.cryptoField.configureUnsealRateCap` is armed by default and counts unseal failures per (actor, table, column). No shipped read named an actor, so every read shared one bucket: once a forged value in a sealed column tripped the threshold, the framework refused that column to every reader for the whole cooldown, five minutes by default. `b.db.from(table).asActor(actor)` names the principal a read is for, and `first()`, `all()` and `stream()` carry it. The chain refuses an actor that names no principal, and refuses null or undefined, since a read with no actor is what happens when the call is omitted. `b.breakGlass.unsealRow` counts against the grant's holder, and `unsealRowAsService` against the API key that opened the bypass.

items.title: A step-up audit row names the principal the decision was about
items.body: `b.middleware.requireStepUp` decides which principal a step-up applies to by reading `req.user.id`, then `userId`, then `claims.sub`, then `sub`, so it serves a principal named by any of the four. The two audit emitters read `req.user.id` alone, so a decision about a principal named by one of the other three was recorded with a null actor: the row said a step-up was required or satisfied and named nobody it was about, which is the unattributed state `b.audit.bindActor` refuses. The four-field chain now lives in `b.auth.stepUp`, which owns the question, and both the matcher and the emitters read it, so a future edit cannot narrow what the audit names while leaving what the matcher matches. `b.auth.stepUp.emitAuditRequired` and `emitAuditSatisfied` take an optional audit sink as a trailing argument, the shape every other audited primitive here already accepts.

items.title: An agent audit row carries its actor whichever field names it
items.body: `b.agent.saga`, `b.agent.eventBus`, `b.agent.orchestrator`, `b.agent.idempotency`, `b.agent.postureChain`, `b.agent.snapshot`, `b.agent.stream`, `b.agent.tenant`, `b.agent.trace` and `b.mail.agent` share one actor normalizer, and it read `actor.id` into both the row's `id` and its `userId`. An actor written as `{ userId }`, `{ username }`, `{ sub }`, `{ principalId }` or `{ email }` produced a row with no actor at all, which `b.audit.bindActor` refuses and which leaves the action unattributed everywhere else. It now reads the fields `b.requestHelpers.actorIdentityKey` reads, in that order, and a string or number actor keeps its own name instead of becoming the system actor.

items.title: Redaction recognizes bytes it did not construct, and a byte body is scanned
items.body: `b.redact.redact` replaced a byte value with its marker only when this realm's `Uint8Array` had built it. A byte array built anywhere else fell past that branch to the plain-object walk, which found no properties to copy and wrote each byte as a numbered key: a six-byte secret came out as `{"0":115,"1":101,"2":99,"3":114,"4":101,"5":116}` where the same bytes built here collapse to `[REDACTED]`. A classifier from `b.redact.classifyDefaults` decided the same way whether a body was bytes, so a body built elsewhere skipped the text scan and returned `verdict: "clean"` for a payload carrying a Social Security number. `b.redact.installOutboundDlp` gates egress on that verdict, so the payload left as clean. Values like these come from operator code that evaluates anything in a `node:vm` context; the framework's own worker boundary does not produce them, because structured clone rebuilds a typed array with the receiving realm's constructor.

items.title: A write-once record stores the bytes it was given
items.body: `b.worm.put` decided whether its input was bytes the same way, so three bytes from another realm were stored as the nineteen bytes of `{"0":1,"1":2,"2":3}` and the record's digest covered that instead. A WORM record is write-once and retained, so a second put cannot repair it.

items.title: A mail filter cannot be walked past its own refusals
items.body: `b.guardMailQuery.validate` refuses a `RegExp` in a filter with `mail-query/regex-not-allowed` and refuses an invalid `Date` with `mail-query/bad-date`. Both refusals tested the realm, so a pattern or a date built elsewhere walked past them, reached the key walk, which is empty for those values, and validated clean.

items.title: A serializer refuses a value it would otherwise write as empty
items.body: A `Map`, `Set`, `WeakMap`, `WeakSet`, `Promise`, `RegExp`, `ArrayBuffer`, `SharedArrayBuffer` or `DataView` keeps its data outside its own properties, so JSON writes `{}` for it and CBOR writes a one-byte empty map. `b.canonicalJson.stringify` refused the first three by name and wrote the empty object for the rest, and callers sign those bytes. `b.safeJson.stringify` wrote `{}` for all of them and raised nothing, which is how such a value reached storage empty through every caller that routes through it; it now raises `json/no-form`, naming the key, at the root and at any depth including inside an array. `b.cbor.encode` wrote an empty map for all of them and for a bare `Date`; `b.cose`, `b.cwt`, `b.mdoc`, `b.scitt` and `b.contentCredentials` sign its output. `b.safeJsonPath.validateContainment` accepted every one of them, after which `b.db` serialized the value to `{}` for the query, and a containment predicate against `{}` is satisfied by every JSON object, so `where({ col: { contains: aMap } })` returned every row rather than the intended ones.

items.title: A limit that is not a number is refused instead of binding nothing
items.body: A limit is enforced by comparing against it, and every comparison with a non-number is false: `entries.length > "abc"` never trips, and `(maxAgeSec || 300) * 1000` is `NaN`, against which every age test is false too. A limit supplied as a string therefore imposed nothing while the configuration said it was set, which is what happens when a limit is read from an environment variable or parsed from JSON without being coerced. Refused at the call now, naming the option: the `maxEntries`, `maxEntryDecompressedBytes`, `maxTotalDecompressedBytes` and `maxExpansionRatio` of `b.archive.read.zip`'s `bombPolicy` and of `b.guardArchive.zipBombPolicy`, which together bound a zip bomb; `maxHeaderCount` and `maxValueBytes` on `b.middleware.headers`, which bound what a client may send; `maxAgeSec` on `b.dbsc.verifyBindingAssertion`, which bounds how long a device-bound session assertion may be replayed and was never type-checked; and `maxResults` on the local `b.objectStore` `list`, which bounds how much of the tree the walk reads. `b.redact.redact`'s `maxDepth` bounds recursion over a log payload and runs where raising is not allowed, so a value it cannot use falls back to the documented default and the bound applies again.

items.title: The vendored-artifact check is documented as what it does, and the checklist reads its verdict
items.body: `b.configDrift.verifyVendorIntegrity` re-hashes every file under `lib/vendor` against `MANIFEST.json` and returns `{ ok, checkedCount, mismatches }`. It does not stop the process, and the framework does not call it. `SECURITY.md` said in two places that it "runs at boot" and that "mismatches abort start", and the operator checklist said to call it "so a tampered artifact aborts start". An operator following that literally calls the function, ignores the verdict, and keeps serving on a swapped crypto bundle with only an audit row to show it. The checklist now carries the lines that read `ok` and stop the boot, the threat model says what the call returns instead of what it aborts, and the assurance case points at the checklist rather than implying the framework acts. That checklist line also passed an `audit` option the call has never had; the audit is emitted on every invocation regardless. The primitive's own documentation named its two throws as `VENDOR_MANIFEST_MISSING` and `VENDOR_MANIFEST_SHAPE` when the codes are `config-drift/vendor-manifest-missing` and `config-drift/vendor-manifest-shape`, so an operator matching on what was written caught nothing; both are corrected and asserted by a test now. A `files` entry carrying no hash was skipped without being counted, which is the silent zero-files-checked pass those throws exist to prevent one entry at a time, and is now reported as a mismatch. Every entry in the shipped manifest carries a hash, so a stock install is unaffected.

items.title: A DKIM "self" requirement names the authenticated identity's domain, not the envelope's
items.body: `b.mail.server.submission.create`'s `dkimRequireMode: "self"` requires a message to carry a `DKIM-Signature` whose `d=` tag names a domain the authenticated identity holds, which is what separates it from `"any"`. The listener resolved that domain from the actor's `domain` field, then from an `id` spelled as an address, and then from the envelope sender. That last fallback let a connection whose actor carried neither field have its `d=` tag compared against its own `MAIL FROM`. The listener reads the tag and does not verify the signature, so a client could write `DKIM-Signature: v=1; d=attacker.example` beside `MAIL FROM:<x@attacker.example>` and satisfy the mode. An unauthenticated connection and one authenticated as `{ id: "u-1042" }` both had such a message queued. The expected domain now comes from the actor alone: its `domain`, the domain of an address-shaped `id`, or the domain of any mailbox assigned to it. An actor holding none of those has no domain for `"self"` to name, so the message is refused. Under the default `identityBinding: "strict"` the envelope sender is already confined to the actor's mailbox set, so those listeners behave as before. A listener running `"self"` under `identityBinding: "permissive"`, or under a permissive profile where `MAIL FROM` needs no `AUTH`, refuses mail it previously queued: give the actor a `domain`, an address-shaped `id`, or a mailbox set. `dkimRequireMode` is now described in the option list beside `requireDkim`, where it was accepted but never documented.

items.title: A CalDAV or CardDAV URL is authorized by one declared principal field
items.body: `b.mail.dav`'s `caldavHandler` and `carddavHandler` compare the first path segment of the URL against the principal they resolve from the request and refuse it when the two differ. That principal was resolved from `req.user.principalId`, then `req.user.id`, then `req.user.username`, all into the single namespace the URL addresses, so two actors named through different fields were one principal. A caller authenticated as `{ username: "alice" }` requested `/caldav/alice/cal1/ev1` and received the calendar event belonging to the principal whose `principalId` is `"alice"`, with the same reach for `PUT` and `DELETE`. Each of those requests is well formed on its own, so no per-request check separates them and the field has to be settled for the deployment. The handlers now read `principalId` alone, and `opts.actorPrincipalId(actor, req)` names the field where a deployment carries it elsewhere; when that hook is set it is the only thing consulted. An authenticated request whose actor yields no principal is refused with 401 rather than served under a shared name, and a hook that throws is treated the same way. `dispatchCaldav` and `dispatchCarddav` are unchanged, since a caller on a non-Express transport passes the principal itself. The module also described per-tenant URL isolation as something it provides while never reading a tenant: it isolates by principal ID, and a deployment whose tenants can hold the same ID returns the tenant as part of the hook's value.

items.title: A valid value is no longer refused for having been built elsewhere
items.body: The same realm test rejected values that were correct. `b.time.toParts` refused a `Date` with `time/bad-input: got object`. `b.safeBuffer.toBuffer`, which nearly every primitive that takes bytes routes through, refused a byte array, and so did `b.acme.revokeCert`, `b.archiveGz`, `b.archiveWrap`, `b.auth.passkey`, `b.auth.saml`, `b.backup`, `b.cms`, `b.contentCredentials`, `b.crypto.xwing`, `b.cwt.verify`, `b.fileType`, `b.mail.bimi`, `b.mail.crypto.pgp`, `b.mail.crypto.smime`, `b.mcp`, `b.objectStore`, `b.sessionDeviceBinding` and `b.vault.wrap`. `b.safeBuffer.secureZero` returned without wiping, and nothing in its return value distinguished that from a wipe. `b.safeBuffer.byteLengthOfIfMeasurable` answered `null`, which a caller reads as having no size to cap, for 1024 bytes.

items.title: A date, a map and a pattern are read for what they are
items.body: `b.compliance.aiAct.logging` recorded a null timestamp for a date it did not recognize. A `b.db` collection filter keyed on a date matched every row, because the date was read as an operator map and a map with no operators in it constrains nothing. `b.mdoc` read a map's members as undefined. `b.middleware.spanHttpServer` left an `ignorePaths` entry inert, so a path it names stopped matching and nothing rejected the entry either; `b.mail.helo` dropped an `extraPatterns` entry instead of adding it; and `b.dev` never matched a redaction or ignore pattern.

items.title: A rejection carrying an error keeps that error's stack
items.body: `b.appShutdown` hands `onUncaught` the value an unhandled rejection carried, wrapping anything that is not an error. The test was realm-bound, so an error built elsewhere reached an operator's crash-reporting hook as a replacement with the same message and a stack pointing into the framework rather than at the throw site. The check also accepted an object that merely claims `Error.prototype` and carries no stack, passing it through as a real error; such a value is now wrapped like any other non-error. `b.selfUpdate`'s rollback path replaced the error it then audited, for the same reason.

items.title: A boxed primitive serializes as the value it wraps
items.body: `b.canonicalJson.stringify` wrote `{}` for `new Number(1)`, which has no own properties, and `{"0":"x"}` for `new String("x")`, whose own properties are indices. `b.cbor.encode` wrote an empty map for both. Each now writes the primitive, which is what JSON does.

items.title: A stale binding assertion names the bound that refused it
items.body: `b.dbsc.verifyBindingAssertion`'s `dbsc/stale` refusal reported the bound the caller passed rather than the one it applied, so whenever the default was in force the message read `iat is more than undefineds old`. It now reads the bound in force.

items.title: The requireBoundKey example returns a key record that names its principal
items.body: `b.middleware.requireBoundKey`'s documented example returned a record with no `ownerId`, and the paragraph above it states that a key without one leaves an audit row naming nobody, because `b.requestHelpers.extractActorContext` reads the principal from `req.apiKey.ownerId`. An operator copying the example got the shape the text warns against. The example carries one now, and the middleware no longer drops the `ownerId` a resolver record supplies.

items.title: A filename overlay is checked against what it does
items.body: `b.guardFilename`'s GDPR overlay was verified by reading the overlay object back, which reports what it declares rather than what it does. It is compared against the default now, where a bidi name is refused and the overlay strips it.

items.title: Twenty-eight namespaces that shipped without a documentation page now have one
items.body: The documentation site generates a page per namespace from the comment block above it, and twenty-eight namespaces had no block, so they had no page: `b.cli`, `b.seeders`, `b.wsClient`, `b.parsers` and its two body readers, `b.secCyber`, `b.sessionDeviceBinding`, `b.otelExport`, `b.websocketChannels`, `b.pick`, `b.lazyRequire`, `b.validateOpts`, `b.frameworkError` and the rest. Sixty-five primitives within them gained a signature, an options contract and a runnable example at the same time.

items.title: An explicit limit of zero is honored
items.body: A limit read as `opts.x || DEFAULT` treats zero as absent, and for a cap zero is usually the strictest setting rather than an unset one. `maxEntries: 0` became 65535, `maxHeaderCount: 0` became 100, and `maxAgeSec: 0` became five minutes, so the tightest configuration could not be expressed. `b.archive.read.zip` already honored `maxEntries: 0`, so the builder disagreed with the reader it builds for. A limit of zero now reaches the comparison it was written for.

items.title: b.cbor.encode names the tag to use for a date
items.body: RFC 8949 spells a date as a tag, and this module already supports tags, so a bare `Date` is refused with `cbor/unencodable` and the message names `new b.cbor.Tag(1, epochSeconds)` for the epoch form and `new b.cbor.Tag(0, isoString)` for the string form.

items.title: Nothing in lib decides whether a value is bytes by which realm built it
items.body: Deciding that a value is bytes has no correct form that tests the realm, so a check covers the whole of `lib/` for `instanceof` against a typed-array view, with no allowlist. Asking the same question about a date or a map does have a correct form, since `x instanceof Date ? x : new Date(x)` handles the other branch, so the existing per-module check keeps the wider set of built-ins and now names every module that decides a type and then stores, signs, redacts, refuses or timestamps the value. Run against the tree before this release, the two report 64 and 42 sites.

items.title: No serializer answers a value it cannot represent with the empty encoding
items.body: Each of the four serializers was corrected separately, each by its own list of named types, and each list was missing a different member. A check now asserts the property across all four instead: for every value whose data lives outside its own properties, the answer must be a refusal and must never be the encoding of an empty container. It carries the differences between the formats rather than flattening them, so a `Map` is encoded by CBOR and refused by JSON, and it asserts the accept side too, so the refusals cannot be satisfied by refusing everything. Adding a serializer means adding one line.

items.title: Four byte parsers that nothing fuzzed now have harnesses
items.body: The fuzz gate requires a harness for every `lib/safe-*.js` and `lib/guard-*.js` primitive, with an allowlist for the ones that are not parsers and a second list for untrusted-byte parsers whose filename does not match. `b.guardImage.inspectMagic` and `b.guardPdf.inspectMagic` each walk a signature table over the leading bytes of an upload, and both were excused as "magic-byte detection covered by safe-buffer" when the signature tables are in the guards themselves and `safe-buffer` does no magic-byte detection. `b.safeBuffer` was excused as having no operator-facing parse path, while `normalizeText` decodes UTF-8 and strips a BOM and the base64 / base64url / hex readers parse text a peer controls. `b.fileType.detect` and `assertOneOf` read the leading bytes of an upload body, a mail attachment or a decoded MIME part, and sat outside both lists because the filename is not `safe-*` or `guard-*`; it is in the byte-parser list now, and both fuzzing workflows carry the target. Each harness was driven over 61 buffers before shipping, covering every signature, every truncation of each, polyglots carrying two signatures, malformed UTF-8 and a megabyte of one repeated byte, with no escape.

items.title: An API name written in lib prose resolves against the framework
items.body: A primitive's prose names other primitives, and nothing checked that those names exist. A check resolves every `b.`-prefixed name written in a `lib/` comment block against what the framework exports, so a renamed or imagined primitive is caught where it is written rather than by a reader who tries it. `@related` references are held to the same rule, and a primitive whose `opts` is the object under test is exempt from carrying an options contract, because there is nothing to document.

items.title: A resolver named for a principal may not take a peer-supplied parameter
items.body: A function named `_actorDomain`, `_principalX`, `_ownerX`, `_tenantX`, `_subjectX`, `_grantX` or `_accountX` answers what the authenticated identity carries. Accepting a peer-supplied parameter alongside that identity gives it a rung to fall back to when the identity carries nothing, and the caller then compares the answer against another field of the same peer input, so the check passes on whatever the peer chose. The gate refuses the shape, with an empty allowlist.

items.title: A CalDAV or CardDAV deployment naming its principal outside principalId sets a hook
items.body: `b.mail.dav.create`'s Express-style `caldavHandler` and `carddavHandler` accepted `req.user.id` and `req.user.username` for the URL's principal segment. They now read `req.user.principalId`, or `req.actor.principalId`, and nothing else. A deployment carrying the principal under another name passes it: `b.mail.dav.create({ storage: ..., actorPrincipalId: function (actor) { return actor.id; } })`. Without that, an authenticated request is refused with 401 rather than served under a name another identity can also reach. When the hook is set it is the only thing consulted, so it also covers a multi-tenant deployment: return the tenant as part of the value and two tenants holding the same principal ID address different URLs. `dispatchCaldav` and `dispatchCarddav` are unchanged, since a caller on a non-Express transport passes the principal itself.

items.title: Name the principal on a sealed-column read and a step-up grant
items.body: Two per-actor mechanisms now ask which principal an operation is for, and refuse rather than sharing one bucket. A read of a table carrying sealed columns takes `b.db.from(table).asActor(actor)`, and the chain refuses an actor that names no principal or is null. A step-up grant minted with `b.auth.stepUp.grant.create({ actor: req.user })` is bound to the field that named the principal, is refused for a principal named by a different field, and is refused when checked without an actor; `create` refuses an actor and a subject together. The existing `{ subject: "..." }` form is unchanged and keeps matching the resolver's chain, so a deployment that does not adopt the binding keeps its current behavior.

items.title: Check that every limit you configure is a number
items.body: A limit supplied as a string, as a negative number, or as a fractional value where a whole one is required is now refused where the call is made rather than ignored. A limit read from an environment variable needs `Number(...)` or `parseInt(..., 10)` around it. The options affected are named under Security above. A limit you leave unset is unaffected, and its default is what it always was.

items.title: Convert a Map, a Set or a Promise before serializing it
items.body: `b.safeJson.stringify` raises `json/no-form`, `b.canonicalJson.stringify` raises, `b.cbor.encode` raises `cbor/unencodable`, `b.safeJsonPath.validateContainment` raises `safe-jsonpath/containment-bad-type`, and a `b.db` collection refuses such a value in a `jsonColumns` column or folded into an overflow column. Each previously wrote or stored an empty object. Convert to a plain object or an array first: `Object.fromEntries(map)` for a map, `Array.from(set)` for a set. A value defining its own `toJSON` is unaffected, so a `Date` still writes its ISO string everywhere except `b.cbor.encode`, which needs the tag named under Changed.

items.title: Verify the vendored artifacts at boot and stop on a bad verdict
items.body: `b.configDrift.verifyVendorIntegrity` reports; it does not exit. If you already call it at boot, read `ok` and stop the boot yourself, and drop the `audit` option if you pass one, because there is none. If you match on its throws, the codes are `config-drift/vendor-manifest-missing` and `config-drift/vendor-manifest-shape`, not the upper-case names its documentation used to give.
